verdict.headline: The energy shock that built over the US holiday is in diesel, not in the price of crude
verdict.label: US markets closed for Labor Day; Brent near $97, WTI above $92, but the diesel crack set a record above $106 against a normal $15-25 and distillate stocks sit 14% below the five-year average
verdict.rationale_short:
US equity and bond markets were shut for Labor Day, so three days of energy news accumulated with no venue to price it. The move is not in the barrel. Brent topped $98 before easing to about $97 and WTI held above $92 — a gain of well under a percent on a weekend in which US forces struck Iranian tankers and Iran said it had targeted three vessels using an unauthorised Hormuz route. That restraint is the evidence, not the absence of it.

The stress is in refined product. The US diesel crack spread, the margin for converting crude into diesel, rose above $106 a barrel on September 1 against a normal range of $15 to $25, and the national average pump price for diesel reached an all-time high of $5.85 on Friday, roughly 56% above the $3.76 average before the Iran war began in late February. The two inventory numbers separate the causes: commercial crude stocks sit about 1% above their five-year average while distillate stocks sit at 104.2 million barrels for the week ending August 28, roughly 14% below theirs. There are enough barrels; there is not enough capacity to convert them. Middle Eastern refineries damaged in the Iran conflict and Russian refining repeatedly hit by Ukrainian drone strikes are two simultaneous constraints on the same step.

That distinction decides what the week's calendar does. August PPI on Thursday is forecast near 5.2% year over year against July's 4.7% actual, and diesel enters producer prices through freight — a cost sitting in the base of most goods rather than in one sector. The print lands with the FOMC in blackout through September 17, so no official can frame it before the September 15-16 decision. Hike odds were near 57% after the August payrolls print and 66% before it.

The evidence cuts both ways on where crude goes from here. Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said a Hormuz shipping agreement with Oman is in its final stages and will be documented with the International Maritime Organization. A deal that reopens transit takes risk premium out of crude and adds no refining capacity, which would widen the diesel crack rather than close it — the pass-through into producer prices would survive a lower Brent. The opposite reading is also available: if the crack narrows alongside crude once transit normalises, the refining shortage was a byproduct of the blockade rather than a structural loss of capacity.

The levels that would change the picture are unchanged because nothing US-listed traded: 4.818% on the ten-year, 5.30% on the thirty-year, 7,700 on the S&P 500 — 19 points below Friday's close — and $95 on WTI. Add $100 on the diesel crack, the level it first cleared on August 17. Brent falling back toward $90 while the crack holds above $100 confirms the constraint is in refining; both falling together says it was not.
verdict.lede_short: With US markets closed for Labor Day, the energy news that accumulated is not about crude. Brent gained under 1% to near $97 on a weekend of tanker strikes, while the US diesel crack spread sits at a record above $106 against a normal $15-25 and pump diesel hit an all-time $5.85. Crude stocks are 1% above their five-year average, distillate 14% below: the constraint is refining, and Thursday's PPI is where it lands first.

supporting_data.label: The US national average diesel price reached a record $5.85 a gallon on September 4, above the roughly $5.82 peak of June 2022 and about 56% higher than the $3.76 average before the Iran war began in late February — diesel enters the cost base of most goods through freight rather than showing up in a single sector, which is what makes it a producer-price input rather than an energy-sector story

The US diesel crack spread rose above $106 a barrel on September 1, a record, against a normal range of $15 to $25, while commercial crude inventories sit about 1% above their five-year average — the shortage is in the capacity to convert a barrel, not in the supply of barrels, which is why crude gained under 1% on a weekend of tanker strikes

EIA put US distillate stocks at 104.2 million barrels for the week ending August 28, roughly 14% below the five-year average — the buffer that would normally absorb a refinery outage is the thinnest part of the complex, and Wednesday's weekly report is the last supply data before Thursday's PPI

Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said a Strait of Hormuz shipping agreement with Oman is in its final stages and will be documented with the International Maritime Organization — a deal reopening transit removes risk premium from crude without adding refining capacity, so it would widen the diesel crack rather than close it

July PPI printed 4.7% year over year, below the 4.9% consensus, and forecasters put August near 5.2% for the September 10 release — it lands with the FOMC in blackout through September 17, so no official can frame the print before the September 15-16 decision

Canada's counter-tariffs on more than 700 US products at rates of 15%, 25% and 50% take effect at 12:01 AM on September 8, covering steel, aluminium, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics — a second cost-push input arriving at the reopen, two days before PPI

watchlist_mentions.note: WTI held above $92 and Brent topped $98 before easing to about $97, a gain of under 1% on a weekend in which US forces struck Iranian tankers and Iran said it targeted three vessels using an unauthorised Hormuz route. The restraint is the point: commercial crude stocks are roughly 1% above their five-year average. $95 remains the regime threshold, and Iran's statement that an Oman transit deal is in its final stages is the cleanest route back below $90.

The most direct watchlist exposure to a refining shortage rather than a crude one. Jet fuel is a middle distillate produced from the same constrained capacity as diesel, and the diesel crack at a record above $106 against a normal $15-25 raises the input cost regardless of where Brent settles. An Oman transit deal that lowers crude would not, on its own, lower this.

Closed 8.26% higher as the Kospi rose 4.61% to 6,995.39, the largest contributor to the move, on a KB Securities estimate placing memory inventories below ten days of supply. That is a broker's estimate rather than a supplier's disclosure; Micron's next quarterly report is the first company data able to test it. The Kospi has still never closed above 7,000, five points away.

Trading at $79,049 late Monday, down 1.66% over 24 hours in a $78,667-$80,430 range (Crypto.com). A fourth session below $80,000 and the only liquid venue that could express the weekend's news, which it declined to do in either direction. $78,000 is the downside reference into Thursday's PPI and Friday's CPI.

trade_setups.thesis: Crude and refined product have separated because they price different constraints. Commercial crude inventories sit about 1% above their five-year average while distillate stocks at 104.2 million barrels sit roughly 14% below theirs, and the diesel crack spread set a record above $106 a barrel on September 1 against a normal $15 to $25. Two capacity losses are stacked on the same conversion step: Middle Eastern refineries damaged in the Iran conflict, and Russian refining repeatedly hit by Ukrainian drone strikes. Iran's statement that a Hormuz transit agreement with Oman is in its final stages is the test — it would lower crude and add no refining capacity.
trade_setups.entry: $100 on the diesel crack is the level it first cleared on August 17 and the line that separates a structural refining shortage from a blockade byproduct. $95 on WTI is the regime threshold; $90 is where Brent would sit if the transit premium came out.
trade_setups.invalidation: Crude and the crack falling together once transit normalises would say the refining shortage was a function of the blockade rather than lost capacity. A distillate build in Wednesday's EIA report would be the first supply-side evidence of the same.
trade_setups.horizon: This week, through the September 9 EIA report and the September 10 PPI print

trade_setups.asset: August PPI on September 10 and the freight pass-through
trade_setups.thesis: August PPI is forecast near 5.2% year over year against July's 4.7% actual, which came in below a 4.9% consensus. Record diesel reaches producer prices through freight, which sits in the cost base of most goods rather than in one sector, so the channel is broader than an energy line item. The print arrives with the FOMC in blackout through September 17, four trading days before the September 15-16 decision, with hike odds near 57% after the August payrolls print and 66% before it.
trade_setups.entry: 5.2% is the forecast the print is measured against. CPI the following morning is the second half: diesel reaches consumer prices with a lag, so a hot PPI alongside a contained CPI leaves the pass-through unresolved going into the meeting.
trade_setups.invalidation: A PPI print at or below July's 4.7% despite the energy move would say the pass-through is slower than the crack spread implies, and would leave the payrolls print as the only hawkish input on the board.

trade_setups.asset: Tuesday's reopen and the cost-push read
trade_setups.thesis: US cash markets reopen after four days carrying the Hormuz escalation, Iran's Oman statement, the Asian memory repricing, and Canada's counter-tariffs on more than 700 US products at 15% to 50%, effective 12:01 AM September 8 and covering steel, aluminium, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. Every one of those is a cost input rather than a demand signal, and they all arrive two days before PPI with the Fed unable to comment.
trade_setups.entry: 7,700 on the S&P 500 sits 19 points below Friday's 7,718.60 close. Whether energy and transport-exposed names separate from the index is what distinguishes a cost-push session from a broad risk move. S&P 500 futures ended the shortened holiday session near 7,717.
trade_setups.invalidation: A broad advance with the index led by rate-sensitive sectors would say the market read the weekend as de-escalation on the Oman statement rather than as accumulated cost. A decline concentrated in the memory complex would say the Asian move was the thing that did not survive US pricing.
